base_method_text.title: DiffDA: a Diffusion Model for Weather-scale Data Assimilation
base_method_text.summary:
The generation of initial conditions via accurate data assimilation is
crucial for weather forecasting and climate modeling. We propose DiffDA as a
denoising diffusion model capable of assimilating atmospheric variables using
predicted states and sparse observations. Acknowledging the similarity between
a weather forecast model and a denoising diffusion model dedicated to weather
applications, we adapt the pretrained GraphCast neural network as the backbone
of the diffusion model. Through experiments based on simulated observations
from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset, our method can produce assimilated global
atmospheric data consistent with observations at 0.25 deg (~30km) resolution
globally. This marks the highest resolution achieved by ML data assimilation
models. The experiments also show that the initial conditions assimilated from
sparse observations (less than 0.96% of gridded data) and 48-hour forecast can
be used for forecast models with a loss of lead time of at most 24 hours
compared to initial conditions from state-of-the-art data assimilation in ERA5.
This enables the application of the method to real-world applications, such as
creating reanalysis datasets with autoregressive data assimilation.
base_method_text.main_contributions: The paper introduces DiffDA, a novel machine learning method for weather-scale data assimilation using a denoising diffusion model. Key contributions include achieving high-resolution data assimilation (0.25°) ready for weather forecasting, creating data assimilation cycles with an ML weather forecasting model, and using a pretrained ML forecast model (GraphCast) as the diffusion model's backbone.
base_method_text.methodology: DiffDA employs a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) conditioned on predicted states from a forecast model (GraphCast) and sparse observations. It uses a soft mask and interpolation techniques to enforce observation values during inference. The method adapts a pretrained GraphCast model as the backbone of the diffusion model.
base_method_text.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted using the WeatherBench2 dataset (based on ERA5 reanalysis data) to simulate observations. The model was trained on data from 1979-2015, validated on 2016 data, and tested on 2022 data. Performance was evaluated using root mean square errors (RMSEs) against ERA5 data for variables like geopotential, temperature, and wind speed. Autoregressive data assimilation cycles and forecast experiments were also performed.
base_method_text.limitations: The method currently only supports point measurements at a single time step as observations, excluding satellite imagery and radar soundings. It also lacks quality control of the input observation data, relying on simulated observations from the ERA5 dataset.
base_method_text.future_research_directions: Future research directions include supporting broader types of observations and multiple time steps using loss-function-based conditioning, adding conditioning of satellite imagery directly into the diffusion model, and investigating possible quality control techniques for input observation data. The authors also plan to explore four-dimensional assimilation techniques.
